set.statement: In people studied from 1967 to 1970, both people given pharmaceutical LSD in medical or research settings and people who reported taking LSD outside them, mostly illicit drugs sold as LSD, the evidence is insufficient to say whether LSD, compared with no LSD or with each person's own sample from before LSD, changes chromosome breakage. Six of the primary studies have been read in full (Cohen, Marinello, et al., 1967; Irwin & Egozcue, 1967; Cohen, Hirschhorn, et al., 1967; Loughman et al., 1967; Sparkes et al., 1968; Tjio et al., 1969), among them the first two studies of people that reported raised breakage after LSD; the others, including the later and larger studies of those two laboratories and the study of LSD given into a vein (Hungerford et al., 1968), are known only through one 1971 narrative review in Science (Dishotsky et al., 1971; figures second-hand; no search method or selection criteria stated; supported in part by the State of California Department of Mental Hygiene and by Mendocino State Hospital, where two of the authors worked; its tables include the authors' own unpublished study, and its second author, W. D. Loughman, was the first author of one of the negative studies, Loughman et al., 1967). What these studies measured was breaks seen under a microscope in chromosomes of white blood cells taken from the blood and made to divide in a culture dish, counted as breaks per cell in some studies and as the share of cells with any aberration in others, in groups of 1 to 46 people, by laboratories whose breakage rates in unexposed controls ranged from 0% to 11.9%; most breaks recorded were of a kind that the review's authors say mostly arises from the culture procedure itself, and they limit their own conclusion to damage detectable by the methods then available. The concern began with Cohen, Marinello, et al. (1967), as Tjio et al. (1969) note, mainly a study of cells in a dish, not of people: LSD added to cultured white blood cells from two donors, whose results were pooled, was followed by 0.050 to 0.368 breaks per cell in 15 conditions of concentration and exposure time, against 0.037 (34 breaks in 925 cells) in untreated cultures from six people, with no statistical test of the difference (the review nonetheless lists it as significant) and, in the paper's own Table 1, no steady rise with concentration; its one patient, a man given LSD 15 times with psychotherapy who had also been treated with chlorpromazine and chlordiazepoxide, had 12% breakage in 200 cells 8 months after his last session, against the 3.7% of untreated cultures from other people, with no sample from before LSD (the same laboratory's later report lists, as its case 37, a man of 52 who had taken LSD 15 times, the last 8 months before sampling, with phenothiazines as his only other drug and 39 breaks in 300 cells; he matches this patient in all but age and the number of cells scored, but neither paper says whether he is the same man). Later in 1967 the first two studies of people that reported raised breakage, both read in full, compared people who had taken LSD with people who had not, with coded slides but no samples from before LSD and no statistical comparison of the groups in either paper. Irwin and Egozcue (1967) found on average 23.6 breaks per 100 cells in 8 men who reported taking LSD an estimated 4 to 200 times (its source not stated; some had also taken cannabis, mescaline or peyote, psilocybin or DMT, not counted) against 11.9 in 9 volunteers who had not taken it (editors' calculation; 95% interval of the difference about 3.7 to 19.7), with overlapping ranges, no women in the LSD group, and the two highest control rates in people with x-ray exposure. Cohen, Hirschhorn, et al. (1967) found 13.2 breaks per 100 cells (566 in 4282) in 18 patients with a history of LSD, every one of whom had also taken other drugs or medicines (amphetamines 15, phenothiazines 10) and whose recruitment and source of LSD are not described, against 3.8 (102 in 2674) in 12 controls without drugs, after two controls with 31.0 and 14.0 were left out for a viral illness that began within a day of sampling (5.4 with them); yet 6 patients taking other drugs or medicines but no LSD (three of them chlorpromazine, two of them boys aged 9) had similar rates, 12.6 on average, no different from the LSD patients (editors' calculation; the paper makes no such comparison); and 4 children exposed to LSD before birth had 11.9 (119 in 1000), compared only with adults. Two other small cross-sectional studies found no excess: no chromatid breaks in 697 cells from 8 people who reported heavy recent use of illicit LSD (7 of them also amphetamines), scored by someone who did not know their drug histories, against none in 112 cells from one concurrent control and 1 in 561 cells from 18 earlier controls of the same laboratory (Loughman et al., 1967); and 2.2 breaks per 100 cells (21 in 937) in 4 psychiatric patients who had taken LSD privately and 1.5 (14 in 914) in 4 patients given LSD in treatment, against 1.6 (15 in 950) in 4 hospital volunteers, with each sample cultured in two laboratories and blinding of the scorers not reported (Sparkes et al., 1968); groups this small cannot exclude a modest rise. The strongest study, Tjio et al. (1969), sampled 32 hospital patients with alcoholism or neurosis before and 1 to 10 days after one dose of pharmaceutical LSD, with coded samples scored by one reader who did not know whether a sample came before or after LSD: the share of cells with chromosome aberrations went from 4.28% to 5.91% on average, not a significant change (P = 0.3; 95% interval of the change about −1.3 to +4.6 percentage points, editors' calculation); 3 patients had large rises (to 23.08%, 43.92% and 14.16%), and the 2 of them who could be retested were back within the normal range 71 and 229 days later (one still 2.32 points above his own earlier rate); there was no untreated comparison group, and 31 of the 32 had been given other medicines in hospital before their first sample. Cohen, Marinello, et al. and Tjio et al. both used LSD supplied by Sandoz Pharmaceuticals. What these designs can show is limited: cells in a dish are not people, blood cells are not sperm or egg cells (none of these studies examined those), and pharmaceutical LSD given in hospital is not street LSD of unknown content. In the review's tallies, of 310 people in 21 reports from 17 laboratories, at most 18 of 126 given pharmaceutical LSD (14.29%) and at most 90 of 184 exposed to illicit drugs sold as LSD (48.9%) had breakage above their control group's average (Cohen, Marinello, et al.'s patient is counted among the first; if he is also Cohen, Hirschhorn, et al.'s case 37, he is counted among the second as well). The early reports of raised breakage in people, from 1967 on, came from three teams studying people who used many illicit drugs (80 of 86 people studied by two of them had raised rates; the first report of each is read, as above, the later ones are not), whereas nine other teams studying similar people (88 people, editors' sum from Table 2, including those of Loughman et al. and Sparkes et al.) found none beyond that in the general population apart from one infant exposed before birth; nearly all of these people used other drugs too (of 77 with raised rates and detailed drug histories, 43 had used amphetamine), Cohen, Hirschhorn, et al.'s patients taking other drugs or medicines without LSD had rates similar to their LSD patients (above), whom the review counts as exposed to illicit LSD although the paper does not say where their LSD came from, and only 54% of 57 street samples sold as LSD contained it in relatively pure form. Among people given pharmaceutical LSD, the review's comparisons with unexposed controls found raised breakage in at most 12 of 70 (17.1%), all but one (Cohen, Marinello, et al.'s patient) reported by one team whose methods the review's authors criticize (as few as 3 of 61, 4.9%, leaving out that team's incomplete data); in 56 people tested before and after, 6 (10.7%) had raised breakage afterwards, 3 of them after LSD given into a vein (Hungerford et al., 1968, as the review describes it) and 1 with a viral infection, and the review says the 5 of these 6 who were retested 2 weeks to 7.67 months later were back at their earlier rates (in Tjio et al.'s own figures, one of their two retested patients was back within the normal range but not at his own earlier rate); only the intravenous study (3 people) showed a significant group change (1.0% to 4.78%), and in Tjio et al.'s study, which the review counts as 37 patients, the 5 volunteers who had used illicit LSD before, reported with the 32 patients, went from 2.81% to 3.57% as printed (3.17% from the paper's own Table 4, editors' calculation), not significantly. In cells exposed to LSD in a dish, 6 of 9 studies found more breaks, mostly at concentrations or exposure times the review's authors judge unreachable in people, and in one study aspirin raised breakage about as much as LSD (9.6% and 10.2% of cells, against 5.0% in untreated cells); in Cohen, Hirschhorn, et al.'s cultures, 7.7 to 17.5 breaks per 100 cells against 3.9, with no statistical test and no rise across a 10,000-fold range of concentrations. On cancer, the review found no significant research, only three case reports of leukaemia or other cancers in about four years, and it says that, as of then, there appeared to be no definite evidence that LSD causes cancer. On birth defects, no malformation had been reported after pharmaceutical LSD and six after illicit LSD (several of the mothers also used other drugs), which the review's authors say may be coincidence; of 14 children exposed to illicit LSD before birth, 10 had raised breakage and all were healthy without birth defects (Cohen, Hirschhorn, et al.'s 4 children, 2 of them with high rates against adult controls and none with obvious abnormalities, belong to a report the review does not cite for this count); and in a series of 148 pregnancies, spontaneous abortions occurred in 37% when parents had used both pharmaceutical and illicit LSD, against 15% with pharmaceutical LSD alone and 20% in the general population, but only 12 of the pregnancies involved LSD during gestation and one woman accounted for 5 of the 10 abortions in the combined group. Animal results were inconsistent: in fruit flies, mutations appeared only at concentrations the review's authors call extremely high; malformations were seen in some mouse strains but not others; and of four pregnant rhesus monkeys given repeated injections at 100 or more times the usual human experimental dose, two delivered stillborn infants with facial deformities and one infant died at a month, which the review calls preliminary but suggestive. In the editors' reading, the review authors' closing statement that they believe pure LSD in moderate doses is not a teratogen or a carcinogen in man goes beyond this evidence. Certainty: very low. Status: mixed.
set.magnitude: Primary studies read in full. Cohen, Marinello, et al. (1967), cells in a dish from two pooled donors: 0.050 to 0.368 breaks per cell in 15 LSD conditions against 0.037 (34 of 925 cells) in untreated cultures, no statistical test (384 breaks in 2678 treated cells, 0.143 per cell, editors' sum); one patient 12% in 200 cells, no sample from before LSD. Irwin & Egozcue (1967): breaks per 100 cells 12.0 to 38.0 in 8 men reporting LSD use against 7.0 to 25.0 in 9 volunteers without it; means 23.6 against 11.9 (378 of 1600 and 215 of 1800 cells; difference 11.7, 95% interval 3.7 to 19.7, editors' calculation; the review prints 23.4% against 11.0% in its text and 11.9% in its table); P < .05 for 6 of 8 and 1 of 9 people, test not named. Cohen, Hirschhorn, et al. (1967): 13.2 breaks per 100 cells (566 in 4282) in 18 patients with a history of LSD and of other drugs or medicines against 3.8 (102 in 2674) in 12 drug-free controls, no test (difference 9.3, 95% interval 6.2 to 12.3, editors' calculation; with the 2 controls left out after a viral illness, 5.4 and a difference of 6.6, 1.5 to 11.7); 6 patients taking other drugs or medicines without LSD 12.6 (mean of six rates; 161 in 1361 cells), not different from the LSD patients (Mann-Whitney P = 0.84, editors' calculation); 4 children exposed before birth 11.9 (119 in 1000), compared only with adults; cells in a dish from 6 donors 7.7 to 17.5 against 3.9 (1009 breaks in 7735 treated cells, editors' sum; the review lists 8725 cells), no concentration-response, no test. Loughman et al. (1967): 0 chromatid breaks in 697 cells from 8 people (95% limits 0.0% to 0.5%) against 0 of 112 (1 concurrent control), 1 of 561 (0.2%; 18 earlier controls) and 11 of 1569 (0.7%; published controls), not significant. Sparkes et al. (1968): breaks per 100 cells 2.2 (21/937; LSD taken privately, 4 people), 1.5 (14/914; LSD in treatment, 4) and 1.6 (15/950; controls, 4); cells with a break 1.4%, 1.4% and 1.5%; not significant (with 4 against 4 the smallest attainable two-sided P is 0.029, editors' calculation). Tjio et al. (1969), 32 patients before and after one dose: cells with aberrations 4.28% to 5.91% (+1.63 points; P = 0.3; lower dose level, 11 patients, 4.05% to 9.26%, P = 0.15; higher, 21 patients, 4.39% to 4.16%, P = 0.8); editors' calculation: 95% interval of the change about −1.3 to +4.6 points, 18 rose, 12 fell, 2 unchanged; 3 rises of more than 4 points (2.44% to 23.08%, 9.50% to 43.92%, 1.48% to 14.16%), 2 retested at 4.76% (71 days) and 1.48% (229 days); 5 volunteers with earlier illicit use 2.81% to 3.57% as printed (3.17% from Table 4, editors' calculation), not significant. Dishotsky et al. (1971), counts without intervals: breakage above control means in at most 18 of 126 people given pharmaceutical LSD (14.29%) and at most 90 of 184 exposed to illicit drugs sold as LSD (48.9%; 45.98%, 80 of 174, without one study's incomplete data); 18 of the 108 people reported with damage had pharmaceutical LSD (16.67%). Illicit-LSD studies: 80 of 86 raised in two early teams' studies (for example 18.76% against 9.03% in 46 people, and 13.2% against 3.8% in 18); none beyond the general population in nine other teams' studies (88 people, editors' sum). Pharmaceutical LSD compared with unexposed controls: at most 12 of 70 (17.1%), as few as 3 of 61 (4.9%). Before and after: 6 of 56 raised (10.7%); group averages 5.7% to 4.9% (10 people), 0.0% to 0.0% (6), 2.81% to 3.57% (5) and 4.28% to 5.91% (32), not significant; 1.0% to 4.78% after intravenous LSD (3 people), significant; 50 of 53 given LSD by mouth (94.3%) showed no increase. Other drugs: 6 patients taking other drugs or medicines but not LSD 12.6% against 13.2% in 18 patients with LSD and other drugs, not significantly different by the review's own comparison (the paper reports none; editors' check above). In vitro: 6 of 9 studies positive; in one study LSD 10.2%, aspirin 9.6% and ergonovine 10.0% against 5.0% in control cells. Pregnancies: spontaneous abortion 37% (pharmaceutical plus illicit LSD), 15% (pharmaceutical only), 20% (general population), in 148 pregnancies with 12 exposed during gestation.
set.population: People whose blood cells were examined from 1967 to 1970. Read in full: cultured white blood cells from two donors and one man treated with LSD in psychotherapy (Cohen, Marinello, et al., 1967); 8 men reporting LSD use against 9 volunteers without it (Irwin & Egozcue, 1967); 18 patients with a history of LSD and of other drugs or medicines, 6 patients taking other drugs or medicines without LSD, 12 drug-free controls (2 more left out), 4 children exposed before birth and cultured cells from 6 donors (Cohen, Hirschhorn, et al., 1967); 8 people reporting heavy illicit LSD use against 19 laboratory controls (Loughman et al., 1967); three groups of 4, namely hospital volunteers, psychiatric patients who had taken LSD privately and patients given LSD in treatment (Sparkes et al., 1968); and 32 hospital patients with alcoholism or neurosis sampled before and after one dose of pharmaceutical LSD, with 5 volunteers who had used illicit LSD before (Tjio et al., 1969). As summarized in one narrative review: 21 reports from 17 laboratories with 310 people, 126 given pharmaceutical (pure) LSD in medical or research settings (many of them patients, some treated with psychiatric medicines) and 184 who had used illicit drugs sold as LSD (nearly all of whom also used other drugs), in groups of 1 to 46 people, 56 of the 126 tested before and after LSD; children exposed before birth reported separately (14 exposed to illicit LSD); also cultured cells, fruit flies, a fungus, rodents and monkeys
set.exposure: Pharmaceutical LSD given under supervision (one to three treatments in the before-and-after studies, by mouth except in one study of 3 people given it into a vein; more in some comparison studies, for example 15 sessions in Cohen, Marinello, et al.'s patient), or self-reported use of LSD outside medical settings, mostly illicit drugs sold as LSD, of unknown content and strength (the source is not stated in Irwin & Egozcue, 1967, or Cohen, Hirschhorn, et al., 1967); in laboratory studies, LSD added to cultured cells
set.comparator: Unexposed control groups (breakage rates of 0% to 11.9% between laboratories), each person's own sample from before LSD (with no untreated group sampled at the same times in the largest study), untreated cultures in the cell studies, or, in one study, 6 patients taking other drugs or medicines but not LSD (Cohen, Hirschhorn, et al., 1967)
set.plain: The LSD chromosome scare began in 1967 with a lab test: LSD was added to dishes of white blood cells from two people, with no check of whether the rise could be chance, and one patient who had also taken other medicines had more breaks, with no test from before LSD. Later that year, two small studies found more breaks in people who had taken LSD than in people who had not: about 24 per 100 cells against 12 (8 people against 9), and 13 against 4 (18 patients against 12). Nobody had been tested before LSD, and in the second study every patient had also taken other drugs or medicines; there, 6 patients on other drugs or medicines but no LSD had about as many breaks as those who had taken it. Two other small studies of people who had taken LSD (8 people in each) found no extra breaks compared with people who had not. The best study tested 32 hospital patients before and after one dose of pure LSD, with slides read blind: cells with damaged chromosomes went from about 4 in 100 to about 6 in 100, a change that could be chance; 3 patients had big jumps, and the 2 retested months later were back in the normal range. It had no group without LSD to compare with. A 1971 review put the raised breaks down mainly to early studies of people using street LSD and many other drugs, and street LSD often was not pure; nine other teams found no rise. All these tests looked at blood cells, not sperm or eggs, and only at breaks big enough to see under a microscope. In a dish, aspirin broke chromosomes about as much as LSD. The review found almost no research on cancer, no birth defects reported after pure LSD and mixed results in animals; its authors' belief that pure LSD causes neither cancer nor birth defects goes further than this evidence.
set.grade.domains.risk_of_bias.note: Primary studies read in full: Tjio et al. (1969), coded samples scored blind before and after one dose, but no untreated comparison group, other medicines in 31 of 32 patients and infections between samples (card sc_tjio_1969, ROBINS-I serious); Irwin and Egozcue (1967) and Cohen, Hirschhorn, et al. (1967), cross-sectional comparisons that found more breaks (8 against 9 people; 18 against 12), with coded slides but no samples from before LSD, recruitment not described, self-reported LSD of unstated source and no statistical comparison; the first with groups differing in sex and x-ray exposure and other hallucinogens uncounted (ROBINS-E high), the second with other drugs or medicines in every LSD patient, similar rates in its own patients taking other drugs without LSD and two controls with high rates left out after the fact (ROBINS-E very high); Loughman et al. (1967) and Sparkes et al. (1968), cross-sectional comparisons that found none, of 8 people against 19 controls and of 4 against 4, with groups differing in other drugs, age and psychiatric illness, illicit exposure self-reported and blinding of the scorers not reported in Sparkes et al. (ROBINS-E high); Cohen, Marinello, et al. (1967), cells in a dish from two pooled donors with no statistical test, and one patient without a sample from before LSD (editors' checklist, high). The later studies that reported raised breakage in groups of people are known only through the narrative review (card sc_dishotsky_1971: no search method or selection criteria; unpublished data, including the authors' own; its second author led Loughman et al., 1967) and cannot be appraised; as the review describes them they were small, with nearly universal use of other drugs, laboratories differing in methods, thresholds and control rates (0% to 11.9%), and no account of whether scorers knew which samples were exposed; one widely deviant value was excluded from a negative group.
set.grade.domains.inconsistency.note: Three teams reported raised breakage in people who used LSD and many other drugs, two of them in first reports now read in full (Irwin & Egozcue, 1967; Cohen, Hirschhorn, et al., 1967), and LSD given into a vein raised it for a time in 3 people (as the review describes it), whereas the other studies read in full found no excess (Loughman et al., 1967; Sparkes et al., 1968; Tjio et al., 1969, with 3 large rises among 32 patients), and most other teams in the review found none either. The explanation offered (other drugs and medicines, contaminated street drugs, infections, malnutrition, culture methods and high control rates) is plausible, and one paper read first-hand bears it out in part: 6 patients taking other drugs or medicines without LSD had rates similar to 18 LSD patients (Cohen, Hirschhorn, et al., 1967); but that comparison rests on 6 people, mostly taking prescribed medicines, and the rest on the review's account and its authors' impressions.
set.grade.domains.indirectness.note: Breaks seen under a microscope in white blood cells made to divide in culture stand in for genetic harm in people; blood cells are not sperm or egg cells, which none of these studies examined (Tjio et al., 1969, p. 855); the cell studies (Cohen, Marinello, et al., 1967, and part of Cohen, Hirschhorn, et al., 1967) are not studies of people; children exposed before birth were compared with adults; hospital patients given pharmaceutical LSD, nearly all after other medicines, differ from people taking street LSD of unknown content; methods of 1967 to 1970; apart from the first two, the studies that reported raised breakage in people are seen only second-hand (METHODS §6.3).
set.grade.domains.imprecision.note: Groups of 4 to 32 people in the primary studies read (1 to 46 in the review); in the largest study the 95% interval of the change, about −1.3 to +4.6 points from a starting 4.28% (editors' calculation from Tjio et al.'s Table 2), includes no change and a rise to about double; with 4 people per group only groups that do not overlap at all can differ significantly (Sparkes et al., 1968); the two studies that found an excess compared 8 with 9 and 18 with 12 people and reported no test (editors' 95% intervals of the differences 3.7 to 19.7 and 6.2 to 12.3 breaks per 100 cells), and the comparison that could separate LSD from other drugs rests on 6 people (interval of the difference −7.3 to 6.1); the review's counts have no intervals.
set.grade.reasoning: Re-rated on 13 November because four of the primary studies had been read in full (Cohen, Marinello, et al., 1967; Loughman et al., 1967; Sparkes et al., 1968; Tjio et al., 1969), so the claim no longer rests only on a narrative review (METHODS §6.3); later that day the first two studies of people that reported raised breakage were read in full too (Irwin & Egozcue, 1967; Cohen, Hirschhorn, et al., 1967), without a change of rating. The human primary studies are observational, four cross-sectional comparisons and one before-and-after study without an untreated group, and start low; the cell-culture studies are preclinical and can only be indirect for people (§5.4). Rated down once each for risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness and imprecision (domain notes): very low, the floor; a strict reading would rate risk of bias down twice, with the same result. 'Insufficient evidence' because neither an increase in breakage after LSD nor its absence can be shown with precision (§6.1): in the strongest study the share of cells with aberrations went from 4.28% to 5.91% on average, not significantly, with a 95% interval of the change (about −1.3 to +4.6 points, editors' calculation) that includes no change and a rise to about double, and 3 of 32 patients had large rises, back within the normal range in the 2 retested; the two cross-sectional studies that found no excess (8 people; groups of 4) cannot exclude a modest rise; the two that found about two and three times the controls' break rates (8 against 9 people; 18 against 12) had no samples from before LSD, did not describe recruitment and reported no statistical comparison, and in the larger of them every LSD patient had taken other drugs or medicines and 6 patients taking other drugs or medicines without LSD had similar rates, so the excess cannot be attributed to LSD; and the cell studies reported no statistical test and no consistent concentration–response. Of the human studies that reported raised breakage, Irwin & Egozcue (1967) and Cohen, Hirschhorn, et al. (1967) are now read in full; they leave the inconsistency and risk-of-bias judgments as they were, with the explanation of the positive findings now resting partly on first-hand data. The study of LSD given into a vein (Hungerford et al., 1968) and the two laboratories' later studies enter only as the review describes them. The review is not independent of one negative study: its second author was the first author of Loughman et al. (1967), and its tables include the authors' own unpublished study. Where the review's figures differ from the primary papers, the primary papers are used: Tjio et al. sampled 32 patients and 5 volunteers, not 37 patients; one of their two retested patients was back within the normal range but not at his own earlier rate; the 5 volunteers' final average is 3.17% in the paper's own Table 4, not the printed 3.57% (editors' calculation); Cohen, Marinello, et al.'s cell study, which the review lists as significant, reports no test; Irwin and Egozcue print no group means, and their table gives 23.6 and 11.9 breaks per 100 cells (editors' calculation), not the review's 23.4% and 11.0% (11.9% in its table); Cohen, Hirschhorn, et al. do not say where their patients' LSD came from, report no test for their cells in a dish, and their Table 5 sums to 7735 treated cells, not 8725; and the review's statement that no positive study showed a relation with dose does not fit Irwin and Egozcue's own table, in which the self-estimated average amount ranks closely with the break rate in 8 people (editors' calculation). Cohen, Hirschhorn, et al. do not say whether their case 37, who matches Cohen, Marinello, et al.'s single patient in all but age and the number of cells scored, is the same man; if so, the review counts him both among people given pharmaceutical LSD and among people exposed to illicit LSD. The claim reports what was measured and where raised breakage was seen, so that a reader can see that the early reports came from people using many drugs and medicines and were not confirmed by the other teams; it does not adopt the review's closing statement that the authors believe pure LSD in moderate doses is not a teratogen or a carcinogen in man, which goes beyond the review's own findings that no significant work on cancer had been reported and that the human data on birth defects were case reports and one series. The cross-study tallies (14.29% against 48.9%) compare different laboratories and criteria and are not used as a rate ratio. Fly and animal findings are labelled and not used for people. Status mixed: the studies disagree, and the explanation offered for the positive findings (other drugs and medicines, street-drug contents, infections, culture methods) is plausible, and supported in one study by a small comparison group, but not established. The new anchors are not yet checked by a second reader, and studies after 1970 were not read and could change the claim. The statement gives no doses.

evidence_set: Cross-sectional comparison of three groups of four: hospital volunteers without known exposure to drugs, radiation or recent viral infection (women aged 21 and 50, men aged 21 and 25); psychiatric patients who had taken LSD privately, usually seeking help after LSD use, all with probable marijuana use and one also DMT and STP (aged 19 to 24); and patients treated with LSD for psychoneurotic reactions (aged 28 to 45; one with probable marijuana use, one Ritalin). The authors note that people who take LSD privately may not know the amount or whether it is only, or really, LSD. Each blood sample was split and cultured in two laboratories, and results were combined because they did not differ significantly. Table 3, breaks only: 1.6 aberrations per 100 cells (15 in 950) in controls, 2.2 (21 in 937) in the private-use group and 1.5 (14 in 914) in the medically treated group; cells with a break 1.5% (14 in 950), 1.4% (13 in 937) and 1.4% (13 in 914). Mann-Whitney tests showed no significant difference between controls and either group (no statistics printed); the authors also report no correlation of damage with total exposure or time since the last dose, without stating a method. Quadriradials were seen only in exposed people (one each in 3 of 8, Table 2), while chromosome interchanges were found in one control and one person in the private-use group. Whether the scorers knew group membership is not reported. Editors' calculation: with 4 against 4, a two-sided Mann-Whitney test reaches P < 0.05 only if the groups do not overlap at all (smallest attainable P 0.029).

evidence_add.locator: Text, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (left column) and 4th paragraph (middle column, continuing in the right column)
evidence_add.extracted: Cross-sectional comparison, undertaken to test the earlier report of more breaks in cultured cells and in one patient (Cohen, Marinello, et al., 1967): 8 volunteers who reported taking LSD-25, an estimated 4 to 200 times, and 9 volunteers who had not taken it, said to be selected at random from volunteer groups by a method not described; one 5-ml blood sample each, the samples given random numbers and processed blind; 72-hour cultures; 200 metaphases classified per person; no sample from before LSD use. Some of the LSD group had also taken cannabis, mescaline or peyote, psilocybin or DMT, in numbers not given. None of the LSD group had x-ray treatment or diagnostic x-rays within several months of sampling; of the controls, one had had about ten x-ray treatments for acne 22 years earlier and one seven diagnostic x-rays of the head and neck 1 to 2 months before.

evidence_add.extracted: Breaks as a percentage of the 200 cells scored (Table 2): LSD group 12.0, 12.5, 21.0, 23.0, 26.0, 25.0, 31.5 and 38.0; controls 7.0, 7.0, 8.5, 9.5, 10.0, 10.5, 13.5, 16.5 (recent diagnostic x-ray) and 25.0 (past x-ray therapy); abnormal cells 11.0% to 34.0% against 6.5% to 24.0%. Chromatid breaks make up most breaks in both groups (Table 1). The text reports a significant increase (P < .05) in six of the eight in the LSD group and one of the nine controls, without naming a test or a reference value; no group means, test statistics or intervals are printed. Editors' calculations from Table 2: means 23.6 against 11.9 breaks per 100 cells (378 of 1600 and 215 of 1800), a difference of 11.7 (Welch 95% interval 3.7 to 19.7; Mann-Whitney P about 0.009); abnormal cells 22.3% against 11.1%; without the two controls with x-ray exposure the control mean is 9.4; 5 of the 8 LSD-group values lie within the controls' range of 7.0 to 25.0. evidence_add.locator: Text, 5th paragraph (p. 313, right column, continuing on p. 314, left and middle columns) and 6th to 8th paragraphs (p. 314, middle column); Table 2 (p. 314)
evidence_add.extracted: The amounts, number of occasions and timing are the participants' own estimates, and the source of the LSD is not stated; the last dose was 1 to 180 days before sampling. The authors say the abnormality rate seemed unrelated to the number or size of doses, but note that the two people without raised rates reported the lowest average amount. Two men in the LSD group had Ph1-like chromosomes, which the authors link to chronic myeloid leukaemia, and three had quadriradials, which they link to inherited conditions with more cancer; no data on cancer are reported. They conclude that it is too early to assess the significance of the findings, yet describe the abnormalities as apparently induced by as few as four doses. Editors' calculation from Table 2: the self-estimated average amount ranks closely with the break rate (Spearman 0.86, n = 8), while the number of occasions (0.48), the largest amount (0.42) and the days since the last dose (−0.28) do not; with eight people, self-estimates of drugs of unknown content and four measures tried, the pattern is fragile, and it does not fit the 1971 review's statement that no positive study showed a relation with dose (Dishotsky et al., 1971, p. 433).

evidence_add.locator: Results › In Vitro Studies, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 1044); Figure 2 (p. 1044); Table 5 (p. 1046); Discussion, 2nd paragraph (p. 1047, left column)
evidence_add.extracted: Cells in a dish, not people: white blood cells from 6 healthy donors, pooled, with LSD added at 0.001 to 10 µg/ml for the last 4, 24 or 48 hours of culture: 7.7 to 17.5 breaks per 100 cells across the 15 conditions against 3.9 in untreated cultures (65 breaks in 1680 cells), with 11.2 at the lowest concentration and shortest exposure (65 in 578); no statistical test of treated against untreated rates is given. Mitosis was 6.2% in controls and lower in every treated culture, more so with longer exposure. The authors take the similarity of the patients' mean rate to the rates at 0.001 and 0.01 µg/ml as a sign that these are the concentrations cells meet in the body, although all five concentrations gave similar rates. Editors' calculations: 1009 breaks in 7735 treated cells (13.0); the highest rate falls at a different concentration for each exposure time, so there is no concentration-response over a 10,000-fold range; the 1971 review lists 8725 treated cells for this study and calls the increase at the lowest concentration significant (Dishotsky et al., 1971, pp. 431–432). Every condition has more cells and breaks than in the laboratory's earlier report, with the highest rate at the same concentrations, consistent with the earlier cultures being pooled here, which the paper does not say.

evidence_add.extracted: Case 37 of Table 1 is a man of 52 who had taken LSD 15 times, the last 8 months before sampling, with phenothiazines as his only other drug and 39 breaks in 300 cells (13.0 per 100). The paper presents itself as extending the authors' earlier report with more patients, but does not say whether case 37 is that report's single patient. Editors' comparison with Cohen, Marinello, et al. (1967, p. 1418): that patient was a man of 51 with paranoid schizophrenia, given LSD 15 times with psychotherapy and sampled 8 months after the last session, who had also been treated with chlorpromazine (a phenothiazine) and chlordiazepoxide, with 12 percent breakage in 200 cells. Sex, number of treatments, interval and phenothiazine treatment match; the age differs by a year and the number of cells scored by 100. If he is the same man, the 1971 review counts him twice: as its single positive person given pharmaceutical LSD (Table 3, p. 433) and among the 18 people of this study it lists as exposed to illicit LSD (Table 2, p. 433).
